title: PRoVeFL: Private Robust and Verifiable Aggregation in Federated Learning

C-a.quote: PRoVeFL is compatible with a wide range of state-of-the-art Byzantine-robust aggregation algorithms (e.g., Krum, Trimmed Mean, FLTrust, norm clipping, MESAS, and more) and further enhances them with verifiability mechanisms that require minimal trust in at least one honest server. ... Since each Byzantine-robust aggregation scheme makes different assumptions about malicious settings and employs unique approaches, we demonstrate PRoVeFL using state-of-the-art poisoning-resistant algorithms such as Krum, Trimmed-Mean, FLTrust, and discuss its extendability to MESAS ... We observe that defenses such as MESAS [29], CrowdGuard [50], and FLAME [51] can be tailored to PRoVeFL.
C-a.locator: Abstract, Section 4 opening, and Section 4.4.4. PRoVeFL IS A CRYPTOGRAPHIC HOSTING FRAMEWORK, NOT A DEFENSE PIPELINE: exactly ONE Byzantine-robust rule is instantiated per round, chosen from a menu (Krum in Figure 4, Trimmed-Mean in Figure 5, FLTrust in Figure 6), and the multi-mechanism-sounding constituents all carry non-defense purposes under Amendment 3. Excised: the multi-key FHE, the deterministic split across servers and the joint multiplicative mask, whose purpose is privacy -- "To obscure structural patterns in encrypted client updates and defend against inference attacks"; the additive blinding, whose purpose is to stop a colluding client-server pair recovering the mask -- "PRoVeFL addresses this through an additive blinding mechanism inspired by the order-preserving encryption scheme of Dyer et al. [49]"; and the commitment-based verification, whose purpose is SERVER integrity, "Protocols focusing on verifiable aggregation (e.g., VerifyNet [17] or SVeriFL [18]) enable clients to detect server misbehaviors by requiring the server to produce cryptographic proofs of aggregation.". The three cryptographic and one robust constituent are applied to the same round, so the row turns entirely on Amendment 3, and the count of DEFENSE-purposed mechanisms per round is one. MESAS, CrowdGuard and FLAME are the only multi-test defenses named and they are explicitly future work, "We observe that defenses such as MESAS [29], CrowdGuard [50], and FLAME [51] can be tailored to PRoVeFL.", notwithstanding the Table 1 caption's stronger claim, "PRoVeFL is compatible with state-of-the-art Byzantine resilient aggregation rules. We demonstrate this by implementing Krum [26], Trimmed Mean [27], FLTrust [28] and MESAS [29]."

C-b.quote: It is a significant challenge to simultaneously achieve all three properties—client update privacy, Byzantine robustness, and server verifiability. Existing methods designed to achieve any of these obstruct or contradict the others.
C-b.locator: Section 1; the paper does give a coverage-style reason, but it is a reason for combining PRIVACY, ROBUSTNESS and VERIFIABILITY -- three security PROPERTIES of the framework -- and not a reason for pairing two defense constituents, which is what C-b's frozen text admits (standalone effectiveness or complementary threat coverage). With one defense mechanism per round there is no qualifying pairing to motivate. The choice among the hosted rules is justified by the CRYPTOGRAPHIC OPERATIONS they exercise rather than by their defensive properties: "PRoVeFL is compatible with state-of-the-art Byzantine resilient aggregation rules. We demonstrate this by implementing Krum [26], Trimmed Mean [27], FLTrust [28] and MESAS [29].", continuing "We also carefully choose these aggregation rules to cover complex operations such as (coordinate-wise) sorting, pairwise comparison, and cosine similarity"

C-c.quote: Byzantine Robustness. How well does the system perform (in terms of accuracy) in the presence of Byzantine clients under various poisoning attacks (Backdoor Attack, Trim Attack) and state-of-the-art Byzantine robust schemes tailored to PRoVeFL? ... Figure 9: Accuracy under Trim and Backdoor Attacks for different aggregation rules (CIFAR-10 L - ResNet-18). P: Plaintext, Rest: Encrypted and simulated with 2 servers.
C-c.locator: Section 6 research questions and Figure 9; the metric is the composed encrypted system's own ROBUST ACCURACY under Trim and Backdoor attacks at adversary fractions 0, 10, 20 and 40 percent on CIFAR-10 with ResNet-18, and the paper reads the composed outcome off it, "Figure 9 demonstrates that all three aggregation rules (Krum, Trimmed-Mean, and FLTrust) maintain high accuracy even when clients’ updates are encrypted and subjected to increasing proportions of adversarial clients (performing Trim [8] and Backdoor [41] attacks). With no attack (both in plaintext and encrypted cases), each method achieves around 90% accuracy. As the adversarial fraction increases to 40%, the accuracy drop is minimal. These results confirm that, despite the added encryption overhead and targeted attacks, the robust aggregation schemes continue to behave as intended when implemented within PRoVeFL.". The paper contains ZERO occurrences of "ASR" and zero of "attack success", so accuracy under attack is the only adversarial outcome available; C-c admits it as robust accuracy

C-d.quote: random mask r preserves relative ordering, this plaintext post-processing exactly reproduces the classical ... mask preserves distance ordering, the plaintext post-processing is identical to the classical Krum rule, while preserving privacy.
C-d.locator: Sections 4.4.1 and 4.4.2. THE ROUTE IS ANALYTIC AND IT IS AN INVARIANCE PROOF OF EXACTLY THE SHAPE OUR PROPOSITION ASKS ABOUT: the upstream stage is the multiplicative mask plus the encrypted-to-plaintext offload, the downstream mechanism is the classical aggregation rule held fixed, and the paper DERIVES that the composed decision equals the unmasked rule's decision because the mask is order-preserving. The first ends mid-sentence at a column interruption -- the extracted stream continues "reproduces the classical The trimmed-mean rule, where all expensive computations, i.e., sorting, are done in the combined plaintext-ciphertext domain", splicing a second sentence into the first -- and the second span BEGINS mid-sentence, its head ("Because the random ... ") lost at the same break, so the two spans are adjacent in the extracted stream but belong to two different subsections. THE EMPIRICAL ROUTE IS DECLINED AND THE REASON IS A MISSING CELL, NOT A MISSING EXPERIMENT: Figure 9's x-axis is "Krum T-Mean FLTrust 0(P) 0 10 20 40 Adversaries", so the PLAINTEXT arm exists only at zero adversaries and every adversarial arm exists only in the encrypted setting. The upstream contrast and the adversarial outcome are both in the figure and never crossed, and the paper's own reading of it is confined to the no-attack point, "Figure 9 demonstrates that all three aggregation rules (Krum, Trimmed-Mean, and FLTrust) maintain high accuracy even when clients’ updates are encrypted and subjected to increasing proportions of adversarial clients (performing Trim [8] and Backdoor [41] attacks). With no attack (both in plaintext and encrypted cases), each method achieves around 90% accuracy. As the adversarial fraction increases to 40%, the accuracy drop is minimal. These results confirm that, despite the added encryption overhead and targeted attacks, the robust aggregation schemes continue to behave as intended when implemented within PRoVeFL."

C-e.quote: Figure 9 demonstrates that all three aggregation rules (Krum, Trimmed-Mean, and FLTrust) maintain high accuracy even when clients’ updates are encrypted and subjected to increasing proportions of adversarial clients (performing Trim [8] and Backdoor [41] attacks). With no attack (both in plaintext and encrypted cases), each method achieves around 90% accuracy. As the adversarial fraction increases to 40%, the accuracy drop is minimal. These results confirm that, despite the added encryption overhead and targeted attacks, the robust aggregation schemes continue to behave as intended when implemented within PRoVeFL.
C-e.locator: Section 6.2.2; the claim names the constituent (the hosted robust rule) and says what it contributes to the combined result -- that it "continue[s] to behave as intended" inside the framework. The analytic version is the stronger one and is quoted under C-d, where the preservation is attributed to a named property of the upstream stage, the mask's order preservation

coder_note:
THIS IS THE THIRD ROW THAT PASSES THE SCREEN AND FAILS C-a, AFTER Byz-Clip21-SGD2M (2603.23472) AND FedEMA-Distill (2603.04422), AND IT FAILS FOR A THIRD REASON: not an excised constituent inside a pipeline, but a MENU. PRoVeFL hosts one Byzantine-robust rule at a time inside a cryptographic shell. The screen was right to include it -- it proposes and evaluates a system that applies cryptographic and robust-aggregation machinery jointly to the same round -- and Amendment 3 is what keeps it out of the DESIGN count, because the shell's stated purposes are privacy, anti-collusion and server verifiability. A5 should present the three C-a failures as three distinct kinds, since a reader who sees only a rate will assume they are the same kind.

THE DISTRIBUTIVE TEST DECIDES THE VERIFICATION COMPONENT, AND THIS IS ITS THIRD INSTANCE AND ITS FIRST ACROSS ADVERSARIES RATHER THAN ACROSS OBJECTIVES. The joint sentence is "The third critical property is the verifiability of the aggregation process. In standard FL, clients are often assumed to trust that the central server honestly performs the intended aggregation. However, a malicious or compromised server could deviate from the protocol by injecting maliciously crafted updates, omitting certain client contributions, or altering the aggregated result. Thus, it is important to verify that the server’s reported global model update truly corresponds to the correct aggregation, while correctly penalizing the malicious updates." -- which, read alone, ties verification to penalizing malicious updates and would make C-a = YES on two defense-purposed mechanisms. The paper distributes it two sentences later: verification exists so that clients "detect server misbehaviors", "Protocols focusing on verifiable aggregation (e.g., VerifyNet [17] or SVeriFL [18]) enable clients to detect server misbehaviors by requiring the server to produce cryptographic proofs of aggregation.". Under the rule articulated on FedEMA-Distill (row 47) and confirmed on SecureAFL (row 50), the distribution governs and the joint sentence is not a purpose statement for verification alone. What is new is that the two purposes here differ in WHO the adversary is -- the server versus the clients -- rather than in what is being optimized, so the test generalizes beyond the fairness/communication/privacy co-purposes it was invented on. Rule 3 points the same way but does not settle it, because the reading changes only the DESIGN rate, a declared secondary, and not the outcome-gated primary, which is NO on C-a under either reading.

COMPOSITION INVARIANCE HAS A NINTH EXTERNAL TREATMENT AND THIS PAPER IS THE ONLY ONE THAT DOES BOTH HALVES OF IT. Analytically it proves that the upstream transform leaves the downstream rule's decisions unchanged, twice, once per rule, and the proof turns on ORDER PRESERVATION -- "random mask r preserves relative ordering, this plaintext post-processing exactly reproduces the classical" and "mask preserves distance ordering, the plaintext post-processing is identical to the classical Krum rule, while preserving privacy." -- which is the same property our own invariance question is about. Empirically it puts a plaintext control beside the encrypted system in Figure 9 and reads the composed accuracy. Nobody else in the frame does both: Fed-DPRoC, SRFed Thm 6.2, CQSA and Byz-Clip21-SGD2M are analytic only; DDFed, SecureAFL, EnCAgg and Secure-CHG's Fig. 6/7 pair are empirical only. A3 MUST NOT BE WRITTEN AS IF THE LITERATURE IGNORES COMPOSITION INTERACTION -- nine treatments is not an absence. The defensible claim, and the one the audit actually supports, is that every one of the nine treats invariance INSTRUMENTALLY: as a property to be preserved, assumed or bounded while the paper validates something else (privacy, verifiability, efficiency, a guarantee), never as an object whose failure could reorder the defenses being compared. PRoVeFL is the clearest case of the instrumental use, because the invariance is what licenses calling the cryptographic layer free, and it holds by construction -- a positive scalar mask cannot reorder distances -- so no measurement was ever at risk.

AND THE EMPIRICAL HALF HAS A HOLE THAT IS THE SHARPEST EXHIBIT IN THE FRAME FOR A4. Figure 9's x-axis is "Krum T-Mean FLTrust 0(P) 0 10 20 40 Adversaries": the plaintext control sits at ZERO adversaries and every adversarial column is encrypted. So the identifying contrast (plaintext versus encrypted, downstream rule and attack fixed) exists only where there is no attack, and the adversarial sweep exists only at one setting of the upstream stage. The two halves of the requirement are in the same figure, one axis apart, and never crossed. This is not the DROP shape (capability present, contrast run in the declined direction) nor the CQSA shape (preservation proved, outcome never measured): it is a MISSING CELL in an experiment that already contains both of its margins. A4 should use it, because it is the cheapest possible counterfactual -- one more bar -- and it makes the point that the absent contrast is usually not an absent capability.

C-d = YES ON THE ANALYTIC ROUTE, FOLLOWING FedSAC AND SRFed, AND THE STRATIFICATION IS WHAT CARRIES THE INFORMATION. If A5 reported only the C-d presence rate, this row would look like SecureAFL's or RKD's, and it is nothing like them: no arm of any experiment varies an upstream defense stage here, because there is no upstream defense stage. The c_d_route field is what distinguishes them and A5 must lead with the stratification rather than the bare rate.
